rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse addresses Muhammad and counsels patience, implying he will triumph over his adversaries as Moses and earlier prophets did.
rows.anchor: This verse is addressed to the Prophet Muhammad, counseling him to patience in a manner that implies that he will emerge victorious over his adversaries, just as Moses and other prophets did

rows.speaker: Ṭs
rows.claim: The true promise may mean God's aid in this world and reward in the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: promise of Divine Aid in this world and reward in the Hereafter(Ṭs)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, the promise may refer specifically to the promise of aid in verses 51–52.
rows.anchor: or to the specific promise given in vv. 51–52

rows.speaker: those who maintain that prophets do commit minor sins
rows.claim: For those who hold that prophets can commit minor sins, asking forgiveness means repenting for those sins.
rows.anchor: For those who maintain that prophets do commit minor sins

rows.speaker: majority of Muslims
rows.claim: The majority hold prophets protected from sin; the command instead urges worship and supplication so God may raise Muhammad's rank and make his practice an example for later people.
rows.anchor: For the majority of Muslims

rows.speaker: Bḍ
rows.claim: Eventide and dawn mean sunset and the time before sunrise; before the five prayers were instituted in Mecca, two prayer cycles were required in each period.
rows.anchor: two cycles of prayer in the morning and two in the evening (Bḍ)

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: Another interpretation takes eventide and dawn as the night prayer, ʿishāʾ, and the morning prayer, fajr.
rows.anchor: Others understand this phrase as a command to perform the night prayer

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Shūrā is generally considered Makkan and placed immediately after Fuṣṣilat.
rows.anchor: Shūrā is considered to be a Makkan sūrah

rows.speaker: Āl, IJ,Ṭs
rows.claim: Some authorities classify verses 23–26 as Madinan because they read them as referring to the Helpers of Madinah.
rows.anchor: vv. 23–26 are from the Madinan period (Āl, IJ,Ṭs)

rows.speaker: Āl
rows.claim: Some add verse 27 as Madinan, reading it as a reference to the poorest members of the Madinan community, the People of the Veranda.
rows.anchor: understood as a reference to the poorest members of the nascent Muslim community in Madinah, known as the People of the Veranda (Āl;

rows.speaker: Āl, IJ
rows.claim: Another view classifies verses 23–24 and 39–41 as Madinan.
rows.anchor: Others maintain that vv. 23–24 and vv. 39–41 are from the Madinan period (Āl, IJ)

rows.speaker: Ṭs
rows.claim: A further view identifies only verses 38–40 as Madinan.
rows.anchor: or that only vv. 38–40 are Madinan (Ṭs)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah takes its name from verse 38, where mutual consultation is described as a characteristic of believers.
rows.anchor: takes its name from v. 38, which describes their affair being counsel among them as a characteristic of the believers

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah is also known by its opening letters, ḥā Mīm ʿAyn Sīn Qāf.
rows.anchor: it is also known by its first two verses, ḥā Mīm ʿAyn Sīn Qāf

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah is framed by continuity of revelation in verses 3 and 51–52, each followed by an assertion of God's omnipotence in verses 4 and 53.
rows.anchor: The sūrah is framed by references to the continuity of Divine revelations (v. 3 and vv. 51–52), each of which is followed by an assertion of God’s Omnipotence (v. 4 and v. 53)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah also treats the continuity between Islamic teaching and earlier religions.
rows.anchor: The continuity between the teachings of Islam and previous religions is also addressed in v. 7 and vv. 13–15

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The closing discussion presents the modes by which God delivers revelation and affirms that Muhammad received it as earlier prophets did.
rows.anchor: understood as a reference to the various modes by which God delivers revelation as well as an affirmation that the Prophet has received revelation in the same manner as did previous prophets

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God is Provider and Sustainer, owns the keys of heaven and earth, and distributes provision by wisdom; this applies to wealth, offspring, and revelation.
rows.anchor: the Provider and Sustainer unto Whom belong the keys of the heavens and the earth (v. 12) and Who provides as He wills in accord with His Wisdom

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most people seek provision elsewhere, take other protectors, argue about God, dispute the Hour, and contest God's signs.
rows.anchor: most human beings seek sustenance elsewhere, taking protectors apart from Him (vv. 6, 9), arguing about God (vv. 16–19), disputing the Hour (v. 18), and disputing His signs (v. 35)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah contrasts those seeking this world's harvest with those seeking the Hereafter's harvest.
rows.anchor: the contrast between those who seek the harvest of this world and those who seek the harvest of the Hereafter (v. 20; cf. vv. 22, 36–39)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah emphasizes that no one has a protector beyond or apart from God.
rows.anchor: no one has any protector beyond or apart from God (vv. 8–9, 29, 44, 46)

rows.speaker: Bg, Ṭ
rows.claim: One interpretation is to answer the person calling people to their Lord, believe in him, and follow him.
rows.anchor: Respond to the one who calls you to your Lord, believe in him, and follow him” (Bg, Ṭ)

rows.speaker: Bg
rows.claim: The caller referred to in that interpretation is the Prophet Muhammad.
rows.anchor: that is, the Prophet Muhammad (Bg)

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: Another interpretation is to respond to what calls people to God, such as faith and obedience.
rows.anchor: Respond to that which calls you to Him, such as faith and obedience” (Q)

rows.speaker: Qu
rows.claim: Responding to God can also mean keeping the covenant with Him and observing His due.
rows.anchor: Responding to God is also understood to mean maintaining the covenant with God (see 7:172c) and observing His due (Qu)

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: The Judgment Day cannot be repelled or averted because once God's decree is made, He grants no further reprieve.
rows.anchor: once the Divine Command has been decreed, God will no longer grant reprieve (Q)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After the decree there is no opportunity for repentance or atonement, as the escape language of 75:10–12 illustrates.
rows.anchor: after the Decree has been made, there is no opportunity for repentance and atonement, as expressed in 75:10–12

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The profligate and disbelievers will be unable to deny their condition and will admit their sins, as elsewhere described.
rows.anchor: will no longer be able to deny their iniquity and will admit their sins, as in 67:10–11

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The day may instead refer to the moment of death, meaning response and repentance remain possible until then.
rows.anchor: A day from God that none can repel can also be understood as a reference to the moment of death

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Jāthiyah is a late Makkan sūrah generally placed immediately after al-Dukhān.
rows.anchor: A late Makkan sūrah, al-Jāthiyah is believed to have been revealed immediately after Sūrah 44, al-Dukhān (JJ)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some consider the entire sūrah Makkan, while others classify verse 14 as Madinan.
rows.anchor: some maintain that the entire sūrah is from the Makkan period, others maintain that v. 14 is from the Madinan period (Āl, IJ, JJ, Q)

rows.speaker: Āl, IJ, JJ, Q
rows.claim: The cited authorities include a view that verse 14 is from the Madinan period.
rows.anchor: v. 14 is from the Madinan period (Āl, IJ, JJ, Q)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah's name al-Jāthiyah comes from verse 28, where every community is on its knees on Judgment Day.
rows.anchor: The sūrah takes its name from v. 28, which states that on the Day of Judgment every community will be upon its knees

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: It is also called al-Sharīʿah because it is the only sūrah using sharīʿah, a term later used for Islamic Law.
rows.anchor: it is the only sūrah to employ the term sharīʿah, which later came to denote Islamic Law

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another name, al-Dahr, refers to al-dahr in verse 24, meaning time, fate, or the passage of time.
rows.anchor: Another name is al-Dahr (“Time”), a reference to al-dahr in v. 24

rows.speaker: Aj
rows.claim: The opening reference to revelation connects to the previous sūrah's statement that the Quran was made easy upon Muhammad's tongue.
rows.anchor: The initial reference to the revelation of the Book can be seen as being connected to the second to last verse of the previous sūrah: We have only made this easy upon thy tongue

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah gives an extended discussion of God's signs, urging reflection and describing the fate of those who deny them; it opens with signs in revelation and creation.
rows.anchor: one of the most explicit and extended Quranic discussions of “the signs of God,” enjoining people to reflect upon them and describing the fate that will befall those who deny them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A brief mention of Israel segues to Muhammad, then reiterates the fate of those who deny God's insights or signs.
rows.anchor: A brief mention of the Children of Israel (vv. 16–17) segues into an address to the Prophet Muhammad (vv. 18–19), which is followed by a reiteration of the fate that befalls those who deny God’s insights, or signs (vv. 20–21)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The rest of the sūrah focuses on deniers of God's signs, the Final Judgment, and the peril awaiting them on that Day.
rows.anchor: The remainder of the sūrah continues the focus upon those who deny God’s signs and the Final Judgment (vv. 22–26) and upon the great peril that awaits them on the Day of Judgment (vv. 27–37)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The statement that this world is all there is expresses disbelievers' rejection of Resurrection.
rows.anchor: There is naught but our life in this world refers to the disbelievers’ rejection of Resurrection

rows.speaker: Q, R
rows.claim: One reading of “we die and live” allows only one life and one death, with no afterlife.
rows.anchor: We die and we live refers to the idea that

rows.speaker: Q, R
rows.claim: Other readings mean that some people die while others live, or that parents die while their children live.
rows.anchor: Some of us die and some of us live,” or “We die and our children live” (Q, R)

rows.speaker: IK
rows.claim: In pre-Islamic Arabia, people commonly cursed the passage of time when hardship struck.
rows.anchor: In pre-Islamic Arabia when hardship befell someone, it was common to say, “Curse the passage of time

rows.speaker: the Prophet
rows.claim: The Prophet forbade cursing time and transmitted God's saying that Adam's son vexes Him by doing so, for God controls affairs and alternates night and day.
rows.anchor: The Prophet enjoined his followers not to do so

rows.speaker: Q, R
rows.claim: The alternation of life and eventual death attributed to time is actually caused by God.
rows.anchor: alternation of life followed by eventual death, which were attributed to the mere passage of time, are in fact caused by God (Q, R)

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: Cursing time for one's suffering effectively curses God, the Agent behind everything that happens.
rows.anchor: when one curses time for one’s sufferings, one is in fact cursing God, since He is the Agent behind all that transpires (Q)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Failure to see time's passage as a sign of God's omnipotence and the meeting with Him results from failure to reflect on God's signs.
rows.anchor: The disbelievers’ failure to understand the manner in which the passage of time attests to the Omnipotence of God and the meeting with Him

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “They have no knowledge thereof” recalls 43:20.
rows.anchor: Thus they have no knowledge thereof (cf. 43:20)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their claim about what follows worldly life has no basis; the text's language about conjecture is compared with 53:28 and 49:12.
rows.anchor: what they do say regarding what follows the life of this world has no foundation, as in 53:28

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Aḥqāf is a late Makkan sūrah; the majority considers verse 10 Madinan, with some also classifying verse 15 or 35 that way.
rows.anchor: the entire sūrah is Makkan

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: Some commentators consider the entire sūrah Makkan.
rows.anchor: Some commentators maintain that the entire sūrah is Makkan

rows.speaker: most commentators
rows.claim: Most commentators classify verse 10 as Madinan.
rows.anchor: most believe that v. 10 is from the Madinan period

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: Some add verse 15 to the Madinan verses.
rows.anchor: to which some add v. 15

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: Others add verse 35 to the Madinan verses.
rows.anchor: and others v. 35 (Aj, Āl)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most of the sūrah was likely revealed around the time of Sūrah 72, two years before the Hijrah.
rows.anchor: The majority of the sūrah was most likely revealed around

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Aḥqāf is the last of seven sūrahs beginning with ḥāʾ and mīm; its name refers to the dunes in verse 21 near where Hūd warned ʿĀd.
rows.anchor: sand dunes in v. 21 as a place near which

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The opening answers disbelievers, calls them to account for rejecting revelation, and affirms that revelation is not a human innovation.
rows.anchor: Al-Aḥqāf begins with a response to the disbelievers, calling them to account for their rejection of the revelation and confirming the nature of revelation as something that is not a human innovation

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: References to the Torah and monotheism transition to the rights of parents, commonly considered second only to the rights of God and His messengers.
rows.anchor: A brief reference to the Torah and those who believed in it (vv. 10–12), followed by an affirmation of belief in one God (vv. 13–14), then transitions into a discussion of the rights of parents (vv. 15–17), which are often considered second only to the rights of God and His messengers

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The discussion of disbelievers leads into Hūd's story, where the people's rejection and destruction warn Quraysh that stronger peoples were destroyed before them.
rows.anchor: A discussion of the disbelievers (vv. 18–20) then segues into a story of the Prophet Hūd, the manner in which the people rejected him, and the punishment that was sent upon them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah recounts jinn who heard the Quran and called their community to follow the Prophet.
rows.anchor: A recounting of the story of the jinn who heard the Quran and then called their community to follow the Prophet

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah concludes with a reminder of God's omnipotence and counsels Muhammad to follow earlier prophets who patiently endured disbelievers' insults.
rows.anchor: A final verse counsels the Prophet to follow the example of prophets before him who patiently endured the insults of the disbelievers (v. 35)
